title: Subnet
summary: A smaller network carved out of a larger one, sharing a defined range of addresses.
quick_actions: Every device on the same subnet can reach each other directly; reaching a different subnet requires a router in between.
The subnet mask or CIDR prefix (e.g. /24) defines exactly where the range starts and ends.

related_pages.label: Computing: CIDR Prefix <-> Subnet Mask Reference

title: CIDR
summary: A compact way to write how big a network is, as a slash-number after an IP address (e.g. /24).
quick_actions: The number after the slash is how many bits, from the left, belong to the network portion of the address.
A SMALLER number means a BIGGER network (more addresses); a bigger number means a smaller network - this is the single most common CIDR mix-up.

related_pages.label: Computing: CIDR Prefix <-> Subnet Mask Reference

title: DHCP
summary: The service that automatically hands a joining device its IP address, subnet, gateway, and DNS server.
quick_actions: Without DHCP, every device would need those settings typed in by hand.
This PirateBox's own visitor Wi-Fi is handed out by DHCP the same way any home router does it.

related_pages.label: Computing: DNS & DHCP: What They Actually Do

title: DNS
summary: The lookup service that translates a domain name (example.com) into an IP address.
quick_actions: DNS is a lookup, nothing more - it doesn't carry the actual traffic, just points to where it should go.
If DNS fails but you already know a server's raw IP address, you can often still reach it directly.

related_pages.label: Computing: DNS & DHCP: What They Actually Do

title: Checksum / Hash
summary: A short fixed-length fingerprint calculated from a file's contents, used to verify it wasn't corrupted or altered.
quick_actions: Change even one bit of the file and the fingerprint changes completely.
Matching hashes confirms an exact copy - it does not by itself prove the source was trustworthy.

related_pages.label: Computing: Checksums & Hashes

title: Character Encoding
summary: The rule a computer uses to turn stored bytes back into readable text.
quick_actions: Garbled/mismatched symbols on screen usually mean the wrong encoding was assumed while reading the file, not that the data is actually damaged.
UTF-8 is the dominant modern encoding and is backward-compatible with plain ASCII text.

related_pages.label: Computing: Text Encoding: ASCII, UTF-8 & Unicode

title: Serial (RS-232/UART)
summary: A simple one-bit-at-a-time connection standard, still common for consoles on embedded/networking gear.
quick_actions: Both ends must agree on the same baud rate (e.g. 9600 or 115200) or the data reads as garbage.
A USB-to-serial adapter is the common way to get a serial port on a modern computer, since most no longer have a built-in one.

related_pages.label: Computing: USB & Serial Basics

title: Polarization
summary: The orientation of a radio wave's electric field - vertical, horizontal, or circular - set by the transmitting antenna.
quick_actions: A mismatch (vertical talking to horizontal) can weaken a signal by 20 dB or more.
A handheld radio held upright is vertical, which is exactly why VHF/UHF FM is a vertical-polarization convention.

related_pages.label: Radio: Antenna Polarization

title: Impedance
summary: A circuit or cable's opposition to AC current flow - RF gear is almost always designed around 50 ohms.
quick_actions: A mismatch between a radio, feed line, and antenna's impedance reflects some signal back toward the transmitter instead of radiating it.
That reflection is what SWR (see below) actually measures.

related_pages.label: Radio: Feed Lines & Common Connectors

title: SWR (Standing Wave Ratio)
summary: A measure of how well an antenna system's impedance is matched - 1:1 is a perfect match, higher numbers mean more reflected signal.
quick_actions: High SWR wastes transmitter power as reflected energy and, at extreme levels, can damage transmit equipment.
SWR matters much less for receive-only listening than for transmitting.

related_pages.label: Radio: Feed Lines & Common Connectors

title: Modulation
summary: How information (voice, data) is impressed onto a radio wave for transmission.
quick_actions: AM varies the wave's amplitude (strength); FM varies its frequency; each trades bandwidth, range, and noise resistance differently.
The Radio Reference page's Modulation Types section covers AM/FM/WFM/SSB/CW individually.

related_pages.label: Radio: Modulation Types (AM/FM/SSB/CW)

title: Simplex
summary: Direct radio-to-radio communication on one frequency, with no repeater in between.
quick_actions: Range is limited to roughly line-of-sight between the two radios themselves.
Contrast with a repeater, which relays a signal to extend range.

related_pages.label: Radio: Simplex vs. Repeater Operation

title: Repeater
summary: A fixed station, usually on a hill/tower, that receives a signal and instantly retransmits it to extend range.
quick_actions: A repeater lets two low-power handhelds that couldn't otherwise hear each other communicate across a much wider area.
Amateur 2m/70cm repeaters commonly carry organized emergency nets during major events.

related_pages.label: Radio: Simplex vs. Repeater Operation

title: dB / dBm
summary: Logarithmic units for comparing signal strength - dB is a ratio, dBm is an absolute power level referenced to 1 milliwatt.
quick_actions: Every 3 dB roughly doubles (or halves) the actual power - a small-looking dB number can mean a big real-world difference.
Wi-Fi/cell signal strength shown as a negative dBm number (e.g. -60) is stronger the closer it is to zero.

related_pages.label: Radio: Decibels (dB / dBm)

title: Declination
summary: The angle between true (map) north and magnetic (compass) north at a given location.
quick_actions: It varies by location and drifts slowly over years - a memorized number can become wrong.
USGS topographic maps print the exact current declination for that specific map in the margin.

related_pages.label: Maps: True North vs. Magnetic North

title: Datum
summary: The specific mathematical model of the Earth's shape a coordinate is measured against - the same coordinates can shift if the datum differs.
quick_actions: WGS 84 is the datum modern GPS devices use by default; older US maps often used NAD 27 - the same numbers can point to a slightly different spot on the ground under different datums.
Always check which datum a map or device is using before combining coordinates from different sources.

related_pages.label: Maps: Coordinate Formats (DD, DMS, UTM, MGRS)

title: Contour Interval
summary: The elevation difference represented between one contour line and the next on a topographic map.
quick_actions: Printed once per map (e.g. 'contour interval 40 feet') - every line up or down that amount in elevation from its neighbor.
Count lines between labeled index contours and multiply by the interval to read an exact elevation.

related_pages.label: Maps: Reading Contour Lines

title: Bearing
summary: The clockwise angle from north to whatever direction you're pointing or heading.
quick_actions: North = 0°, East = 90°, South = 180°, West = 270°.
Specify whether a bearing is true or magnetic - they can differ by the local declination angle.

related_pages.label: Maps: Cardinal Directions & Compass Bearings

title: Latitude / Longitude
summary: The universal coordinate pair for any point on Earth - how far north/south (latitude) and east/west (longitude) of two reference lines.
quick_actions: Always written latitude first, then longitude (e.g. 40.7128° N, 74.0060° W).
Every other coordinate format (DMS, UTM, MGRS) is built on or converts to/from this pair.

related_pages.label: Maps: Latitude & Longitude Basics

title: UTM
summary: Universal Transverse Mercator - divides the world into 60 numbered zones, giving position as a meters-based easting/northing.
quick_actions: Common on USGS topographic maps as an alternative to latitude/longitude.
Distances in UTM are in plain meters within a zone, which some people find easier for measuring than degrees.

related_pages.label: Maps: Coordinate Formats (DD, DMS, UTM, MGRS)

title: MGRS
summary: Military Grid Reference System - the same UTM grid, but identifies the 100km square with letters instead of numbers.
quick_actions: Common on military/tactical maps rather than civilian topo maps.
Read a grid reference "right, then up" - easting digits first, then northing.

related_pages.label: Maps: Coordinate Formats (DD, DMS, UTM, MGRS)

title: Voltage
summary: Electrical potential difference - the "pressure" that pushes current through a circuit, measured in volts.
quick_actions: V = I x R (Ohm's Law) - voltage, current, and resistance are always related this way.
A circuit needs a closed loop for voltage to actually drive any current.

related_pages.label: Field Tools: Electrical & Ohm's Law Reference

title: Current
summary: The actual flow of electric charge through a circuit, measured in amps.
quick_actions: I = V / R (Ohm's Law).
Wire gauge (AWG) is chosen based on how much current a conductor needs to carry safely - see the AWG ampacity table.

related_pages.label: Field Tools: Electrical & Ohm's Law Reference

title: Resistance
summary: How much a component opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms.
quick_actions: R = V / I (Ohm's Law).
Resistance should only be measured on a de-energized, disconnected component - see Multimeter & Measurement Basics.

related_pages.label: Field Tools: Electrical & Ohm's Law Reference

title: Power (Electrical)
summary: The rate of energy use or transfer in a circuit, measured in watts.
quick_actions: P = V x I - volts times amps equals watts.
A battery's runtime for a given load is roughly its watt-hour capacity divided by the load's wattage.

related_pages.label: Field Tools: Electrical & Ohm's Law Reference

title: SI Prefix
summary: A standard multiplier (kilo, milli, mega, etc.) that means the same thing regardless of which unit it's attached to.
quick_actions: Once you know "milli" means divided by 1,000, that's true for milliamps, milliliters, and milliseconds alike.
Radio frequencies use kHz/MHz/GHz; storage uses similar-looking but different, binary-based prefixes (see the Storage/data section).

related_pages.label: Field Tools: SI Prefixes
